name: degradation-trap
notes:
A 60s load pulse the fleet never recovers from — even with a real, working autoscaler free to scale 2-20 (rk6's self-inflicted degradation model, not a fault or an autoscaler failure). This is the free-scaling counterpart to the earlier fixed-instance-count cut: the autoscaler DOES react here, which is the point — it just reacts into a new, permanently degraded equilibrium instead of recovery.

Healthy baseline: 300rps needs ~1.5 instances at the default 50% CPU target (400rps/instance CPU-bound ceiling), comfortably under min=initial=2 — quiet period is genuinely healthy: 100ms latency, 0% errors, 2 instances, no scale-up needed.

At t=180 the pulse hits 800rps for 60s — 400rps/instance while still at 2 instances. Concurrency per instance shoots past the 30-outstanding threshold, `step` degradation snaps the cpu-step multiplier to 8x. Longer holds mean more outstanding at the next arrival, which is already past 30, so the multiplier stays clamped — and because BOTH io and cpu steps are stretched (`degradationTarget` left at its 'all' default), the same real work now genuinely occupies the CPU pool 8x longer too: the CPU metric isn't lying, it honestly reads high.

The autoscaler does what it's supposed to: it sees the spike, scales out. Measured (seed 1, this exact preset): 2 -> 4 -> 5 instances by t~400, then settles and holds at 5 for the rest of the 3000s+ horizon (checked well past 1800s while tuning). Why it stops at 5, not 2 (healthy) or 20 (max): a degraded instance's effective capacity is workers/serviceTime = 50 / 0.8s = 62.5rps; 5 of them give ~312rps, just enough that the reported CPU metric settles right around the 50% target (~49%) — the algorithm is satisfied. It never sees a reason to add a 6th. Meanwhile real users see mean latency ~7.6s and a persistent ~7% error rate (queue-full rejections), forever — the autoscaler solved its own metric, not the incident.

Control check: the identical run with `degradationShape: 'none'` recovers fully and immediately once the pulse ends — back to 2 instances, 0% errors, 100ms latency. The trap is purely the degradation model; the autoscaler's range/behavior is unchanged between runs.

Why this is worse than it looks: unlike a hung/spinning instance's `hungCpu` lie (foh.4's territory), nothing here is dishonest. Every signal the autoscaler reads is real. The failure is that per-instance load-response has a cliff that scaling out capacity doesn't undo once crossed — you can buy your way to a new equilibrium, but not back to health, without the once-degraded instances being replaced (this preset never gives it a fault-recovery or instance-replacement path — that's a natural next variant).
